title: Carbon: how one kind of atom builds sugar, fuel, plastic and living things

summary.text: Heat a piece of sugar, bread or wax and it turns black. What is the black stuff? In this lesson you will heat kitchen things to see which hold carbon, compare glucose, cornflour and cotton, and put carbon chains in order from cooking gas to candle wax.
summary.art: An old black tawa on a gas stove with eight small heaps on a sheet of foil, where the heap of sugar has turned into a black bubbly crust and the heap of salt is still white.

intro.hook: Sugar is white, and a cotton thread is white. Heat either one on a hot tawa and it turns black. Where does the black come from?
intro.text: Many things go black when they get too hot: a forgotten dosa, a roti left on the flame, milk that boils dry. Salt never does. In this lesson you find out what the black solid is and why only some things leave it. You heat eight kitchen things side by side. You build molecules on paper with atoms that make one, two or four bonds. You also test glucose, cornflour and cotton, which are three materials built from one and the same ring of atoms.
intro.art: A girl looking at a burnt black dosa on a tawa, with a heap of white salt and a heap of white sugar on the counter beside her.

outcomes: I can say that carbon is an element, and that each carbon atom makes four bonds.
I can explain why four strong bonds let carbon atoms build chains, branches and rings.
I can test which things at home hold carbon chains, by heating them and looking for a black solid.
I can explain how the length of a carbon chain changes a fuel, from cooking gas to candle wax.
I can explain how glucose rings join into the long chains of starch and cellulose.
I can name the carbon frame in fuels, sugars, plastics and living bodies, and say where each one came from.
I can tell how people found out that the substances of living things follow the same chemistry as everything else.

terms.meaning: The smallest piece of an element. Atoms are far too small to see.
terms.example: A grain of sugar holds many billions of atoms of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
terms.art: A grain of sugar with a magnifying circle showing it is made of tiny balls of three colours.

terms.meaning: A substance made of only one kind of atom.
terms.example: Carbon, oxygen, iron and gold are elements. Water is not, because it has two kinds of atom.
terms.art: Four small heaps labelled carbon, iron, gold and sulfur, each drawn with dots of a single colour.

terms.meaning: An element whose atoms each make four bonds. Charcoal, soot, pencil graphite and diamond are forms of carbon.
terms.example: The black on a burnt roti is mostly carbon.
terms.art: A lump of charcoal, a pencil and a diamond in a row, each with an arrow to the same small black ball.

terms.meaning: The hold that joins one atom to another atom.
terms.example: In a molecule of cooking gas, bonds hold carbon atoms to hydrogen atoms.
terms.art: Two small balls joined by a short stick.

terms.meaning: A group of atoms joined together by bonds.
terms.example: A molecule of water is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
terms.art: One larger red ball with two small white balls joined to it by sticks.

terms.meaning: A row of carbon atoms, each bonded to the next.
terms.example: A molecule in petrol has a chain of about 8 carbon atoms. A molecule in candle wax has about 25.
terms.art: A zigzag row of eight black balls joined by sticks, with small white balls on the outside.

terms.meaning: A chain of atoms whose two ends are joined, so that the atoms form a closed loop.
terms.example: A molecule of glucose is a ring of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom.
terms.art: Six balls joined into a closed hexagon, five black and one red.

terms.meaning: The pattern in which the carbon atoms of a molecule are joined: straight, branched or in a ring.
terms.example: Five carbon atoms can be joined in a straight row, in a row with one branch, or as a cross.
terms.art: Three small drawings of five black balls: a straight row, a row with a side branch, and a cross shape.

terms.meaning: A substance whose molecules are made of only carbon and hydrogen atoms.
terms.example: Cooking gas, petrol, diesel and candle wax are hydrocarbons.
terms.art: A gas cylinder, a petrol pump and a candle in a row, each with a small chain of black and white balls above it.

terms.meaning: Turning black from heat. Heat drives the other atoms out as gases, and a solid that is mostly carbon stays behind.
terms.example: The bottom of a dosa chars when the tawa is too hot.
terms.art: A dosa on a tawa with one black patch and thin smoke rising from it.

terms.meaning: The black solid left when wood is heated with very little air. It is mostly carbon.
terms.example: The ironing man's coal iron and many roadside corn stalls burn charcoal.
terms.art: A heavy iron box for ironing clothes, open at the top, with glowing black lumps of charcoal inside.

terms.meaning: A simple sugar. Each molecule is one small ring with 6 carbon atoms in all.
terms.example: Glucose powder stirred into water gives a sweet drink of glucose. Your blood carries glucose to every cell.
terms.art: A spoon of white powder beside a tumbler of water, with a small hexagon ring drawn above the spoon.

terms.meaning: A food store made by plants. Each molecule is a long chain of glucose rings.
terms.example: Rice, potato, cornflour and atta are mostly starch.
terms.art: A long coiled chain of small hexagons beside a heap of rice.

terms.meaning: The material of plant cell walls. Each molecule is a long, straight chain of glucose rings.
terms.example: Cotton, paper and the hard part of wood are mostly cellulose.
terms.art: Several straight chains of hexagons lying side by side, beside a ball of cotton.

terms.meaning: The study of substances built on chains and rings of carbon atoms.
terms.example: A chemist who designs a new medicine or a new plastic is doing organic chemistry.
terms.art: A woman chemist in a lab coat drawing a chain of hexagons on a glass board.

explanations.definition: Carbon is an element. Every carbon atom is the same kind of atom. Heating or mixing cannot break carbon into anything simpler.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms, and there are about a hundred kinds. A substance made of only one kind of atom is called an element. Carbon is one of the elements. You have already met carbon in several forms. Charcoal and the soot from a lamp are mostly carbon. The grey core of a pencil is graphite, which is carbon atoms joined in flat sheets. A diamond is carbon atoms joined in a network where every atom holds four others. Graphite is soft and diamond is very hard, yet both are pure carbon. The atoms are the same, and only the way they are joined is different. Carbon atoms also sit inside many substances that are not black at all. Sugar, cotton, oil, wax and plastic all hold carbon joined to other atoms. About 18 kilograms of every 100 kilograms of a human body is carbon. Only oxygen makes up more of you.
examples: Charcoal, soot, pencil graphite and diamond are all forms of carbon.
White sugar holds carbon atoms joined to hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
A child who weighs 30 kilograms holds more than 5 kilograms of carbon.
explanations.art: A pencil, a lump of charcoal and a diamond ring, each with a zoom circle showing black balls joined in a different pattern: flat sheets, a jumble and a tight network.

explanations.concept: Each carbon atom makes four bonds
explanations.definition: A bond is the hold between two atoms. A carbon atom makes four bonds, a hydrogen atom makes one, and an oxygen atom makes two.
explanations.description: Atoms join to each other by bonds. Each kind of atom makes a set number of bonds. A hydrogen atom makes one bond. An oxygen atom makes two, and a nitrogen atom makes three. A carbon atom makes four. In the activity One Bond or Four, you draw molecules with these rules. Two hydrogen atoms can join. Then neither of them has a bond left over, so the molecule stops at just two atoms. A carbon atom is different. One carbon atom can hold four hydrogen atoms. This molecule is called methane, and it is the main gas in piped cooking gas. A carbon atom can also use one bond to hold a second carbon atom and still have three bonds free. The second carbon atom can hold a third, and so on. So the chain can keep growing. There is a second reason carbon builds chains. The bond between two carbon atoms is strong, so a long row of carbon atoms does not fall apart easily. Rows of oxygen atoms do fall apart, which is why long oxygen chains are not found.
examples: Methane is one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms.
Water is one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms.
In the gas propane, three carbon atoms in a row hold eight hydrogen atoms.
explanations.art: Three balls in a row: a small white one with one stick, a red one with two sticks and a black one with four sticks pointing in four directions.

explanations.definition: Carbon atoms can join in a straight chain, in a chain with branches, or in a closed ring. The pattern is called the carbon skeleton.
explanations.description: A carbon atom in the middle of a chain uses two bonds to hold its two neighbours. It still has two bonds left. Each of those can hold a hydrogen atom, or it can hold another carbon atom and start a branch. The two ends of a chain can also bond to each other and close into a ring. So carbon atoms can be arranged in a huge number of ways. In the activity Five Carbons, you find that five carbon atoms can be joined in three different skeletons. Each one is a real liquid with its own boiling point: 36, 28 and 10 degrees Celsius. All three have exactly the same atoms, 5 carbon and 12 hydrogen. Substances like these, with the same atoms joined in different patterns, are called isomers. Ten carbon atoms can make 75 different skeletons. Chemists have recorded more than 100 million different substances, and most of them are built on carbon chains or rings.
examples: Butane, a gas in the LPG cylinder, is a straight chain of four carbon atoms.
Five carbon atoms make three different skeletons: a row, a row with one branch, and a cross.
A glucose molecule holds a ring. So does the molecule that gives camphor its smell.
explanations.art: Three skeletons drawn with black balls and sticks: a straight zigzag chain, a chain with a branch and a six-sided ring.

explanations.concept: Why some things turn black when they are heated
explanations.definition: Charring is turning black from heat. Heat drives hydrogen and oxygen out of a carbon-chain substance as gases. A black solid that is mostly carbon stays behind.
explanations.description: In the experiment The Black Inside, you heat eight things on a tawa. Sugar, atta, cotton thread, paper and dry onion skin turn black. Salt, baking soda and a steel coin do not. The five that turn black were all made by plants. Their molecules are chains and rings of carbon atoms with hydrogen and oxygen atoms attached. Strong heat breaks these molecules. The hydrogen and oxygen leave as water vapour and other gases, which is some of the smoke you see. Many carbon atoms stay behind, bonded to each other, as a black solid. This is called charring. Salt holds no carbon, so it has nothing black to leave. Baking soda is a puzzle, because it does hold carbon. But each of its carbon atoms sits alone, held by oxygen atoms. When baking soda is heated, that carbon leaves as carbon dioxide gas. So a black solid is a sign of carbon atoms that were joined in chains or rings.
examples: Milk that boils dry leaves a black crust on the pan.
A roti held on the flame too long gets black spots.
Salt heated on a tawa stays white, however long you wait.
explanations.art: A sugar molecule drawn as rings of black, white and red balls over a flame, with the white and red balls rising as steam and the black balls staying joined below.

explanations.concept: Fuels are carbon chains, and the length of the chain matters
explanations.definition: A hydrocarbon is a substance made only of carbon and hydrogen. Cooking gas, petrol, diesel and wax are hydrocarbons with chains of different lengths.
explanations.description: The gas in a kitchen pipe is mostly methane, with 1 carbon atom in each molecule. The LPG in a cylinder is propane and butane, with 3 and 4 carbon atoms. Petrol molecules have about 5 to 12 carbon atoms. Kerosene molecules have about 10 to 16, and diesel molecules are a little longer. Candle wax molecules have about 20 to 40. Short chains hold on to each other weakly, so the substance is a gas. Longer chains hold on to each other along their whole length. So the substance is a liquid, then a thick liquid, then a solid. You sort these in the game Chain Line. Most of these fuels come from petroleum and natural gas. Petroleum and natural gas formed from tiny sea plants and other sea creatures that were buried for millions of years. Coal formed from buried swamp forests. When a hydrocarbon burns, its carbon joins with oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide, and its hydrogen becomes water. The carbon dioxide stays in the air and traps heat. That is why burning fuels is warming the Earth.
examples: Methane, with 1 carbon atom, boils at 162 degrees below zero.
Octane in petrol, with 8 carbon atoms, is a liquid that boils at 126 degrees Celsius.
Candle wax, with about 25 carbon atoms in a chain, is a solid in the room.
explanations.art: A row from left to right: a blue gas flame, an LPG cylinder, a petrol pump, a diesel lorry and a candle, with a carbon chain above each one that gets longer along the row.

explanations.concept: Sugars are rings, and rings join into chains
explanations.definition: Glucose is a sugar whose molecule is one small ring. Starch and cellulose are long chains made of many glucose rings joined together.
explanations.description: A glucose molecule has 6 carbon atoms, 12 hydrogen atoms and 6 oxygen atoms. Five of the carbon atoms and one oxygen atom form a ring. Plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light. Then they join the rings together. Each time two rings join, one molecule of water is released. Rings joined one way make starch. A starch chain coils, and the plant packs the coils into tiny grains as a food store. Rings joined the other way make cellulose, where every second ring is turned over. A cellulose chain is straight, and straight chains lie side by side and hold each other tightly. That makes strong fibres, such as cotton. In the experiment One Ring, Three Materials, you test all three. Glucose dissolves and tastes sweet. Cornflour, which is starch, clouds cold water and thickens hot water. Cotton does neither. Table sugar is two rings joined: one glucose and one ring of a sugar called fructose.
examples: Glucose powder is single rings. It dissolves at once and tastes sweet.
Rice and potato are mostly starch, a coiled chain of glucose rings.
A cotton shirt is mostly cellulose, a straight chain of thousands of glucose rings.
explanations.art: One small hexagon on the left, a coiled chain of hexagons in the middle and several straight chains of hexagons lying side by side on the right, labelled glucose, starch and cellulose.

explanations.concept: Plastics are very long carbon chains made by people
explanations.definition: A plastic is a material made of very long molecules. In most plastics, the frame of each molecule is a chain of carbon atoms.
explanations.description: The plastic of a milk packet is called polythene. Factories make it from a gas called ethene, which has 2 carbon atoms in each molecule. The ethene comes from petroleum or natural gas. In the factory, thousands of ethene molecules are joined end to end. The result is a chain with many thousands of carbon atoms. A polythene chain is built like candle wax, but it is hundreds of times longer. Long chains tangle and hold each other, so the plastic is tough and bends without breaking. Polyester, nylon and the plastic of water bottles also have carbon frames. Their chains hold a few oxygen or nitrogen atoms too. Plastics are light, cheap and waterproof. They are also a problem. Soil microbes have enzymes, which are the tools their cells use to cut molecules. These enzymes cut the chains of wood and food. Almost no microbe has an enzyme for a chain that people invented less than a hundred years ago. So plastic stays in the soil and the sea for a very long time.
examples: A milk packet and a carry bag are polythene.
A water bottle is a plastic called PET. A polyester sari is the same plastic spun into thread.
A nylon rope is a carbon chain with nitrogen atoms in it.
explanations.art: A milk packet with a zoom circle showing very long tangled chains of black balls, beside a candle with a zoom circle showing short chains of the same kind.

explanations.concept: Living bodies are built on carbon chains and rings
explanations.definition: The main substances of every living body are carbon-chain molecules: sugars, starch and cellulose, fats, proteins and DNA.
explanations.description: A fat molecule has three carbon chains, each usually 12 to 18 carbon atoms long. A protein is a long chain built from small carbon units called amino acids. Muscles, hair, silk and enzymes are proteins. DNA carries the instructions for building a body, and its long frame holds a carbon ring in every step. So a mango tree, a crow, a mushroom and a child are all built on carbon. Plants take their carbon from the air. A leaf takes in carbon dioxide and joins the carbon into glucose. Animals, including humans, cannot do this. We get our carbon by eating plants, or by eating other animals who ate plants. We give carbon back with every breath, as carbon dioxide. A tree may hold a carbon atom for a hundred years. Then the wood rots or burns, and the atom returns to the air. You follow one atom on such a journey in the game Carbon Trail.
examples: Coconut oil and ghee are fats, with three carbon chains in each molecule.
The protein in dal and in egg is a chain of amino acids.
A banyan tree built their trunk from carbon dioxide taken out of the air.
explanations.art: A mango tree, a crow, a mushroom and a child standing together, each with a small chain of black balls drawn inside the outline of the body.

explanations.concept: Carbon atoms were made inside stars
explanations.definition: Carbon atoms are made in the hot centres of old stars. There, three helium atoms are pressed together into one carbon atom.
explanations.description: The first stars were made of hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements. There was no carbon. Deep inside a star, hydrogen atoms are pressed together into helium, and this gives the star its light. When an old star runs low on hydrogen, the centre grows even hotter. Then three helium atoms can join into one carbon atom. This step is hard, because all three must meet at almost the same moment. In 1953 the astronomer Fred Hoyle worked out something about this step. It can only happen if carbon atoms have one particular high-energy state. A team in California tested carbon and found that state, just as he had predicted. When old stars die, they throw their carbon out into space. New stars and planets form from that dust and gas. In 1957 Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle showed how stars make nearly all the elements. So the carbon in sugar, in a pencil and in you is older than the Sun. It was made in stars that died before the Sun was born.
examples: The Sun is turning hydrogen into helium now. It will make carbon near the end of its life.
Dust clouds in space hold carbon thrown out by old stars.
In 2010, astronomers found balls of 60 carbon atoms in the gas around a dying star.
explanations.art: A large red star throwing off shells of glowing gas, with small black balls drifting outward towards a new blue planet.

explanations.concept: Could living things be built on another element?
explanations.description: Every living being found so far is built on carbon. Scientists have asked whether this must be so. Silicon is the usual other choice, because a silicon atom also makes four bonds. Sand and most rocks are silicon joined with oxygen. Nobody has found life on another world yet, so the question is open. Here are the main views.
examples: Silicon sits just below carbon in the table of elements, and makes four bonds.
Sand is silicon bonded to oxygen in a hard network.
Space telescopes find many carbon molecules in gas clouds, and few silicon chains.

perspectives.explanation: Carbon is the best builder by far. Bonds between silicon atoms are weaker, so long silicon chains break apart in water and in air. When carbon burns it makes a gas, which a body can breathe out. When silicon burns it makes a solid like sand.

perspectives.who: Some astrobiologists, who study the chances of life on other worlds
perspectives.explanation: We know only one example of life, the life on Earth. In very cold places with no water, other chemistry might work. We should not rule out what we have not looked for.

People already make silicon chains with oxygen between the silicon atoms. These are the silicones in bathroom sealant and baking moulds. They are stable, but they form far fewer shapes than carbon does.

explanations.art: Two imagined creatures side by side under a strange sky, one drawn with black chains inside the body and one with grey crystal shapes, and a large question mark between them.

agreed.text: Carbon is an element, and charcoal, graphite and diamond are all forms of carbon.
agreed.evidence: In 1797 Smithson Tennant burned a diamond in a closed vessel. It made the same amount of the same gas as an equal weight of charcoal.

agreed.text: A carbon atom makes four bonds, and carbon atoms bond to each other in chains and rings.
agreed.evidence: August Kekulé and Archibald Couper each proposed this in 1858. X-ray pictures of crystals later showed the atoms in exactly these positions.

agreed.text: The substances of living things can be made from substances that were never alive.
agreed.evidence: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a substance found in urine, from a mineral salt. Chemists now make sugars, vitamins and medicines in the same way.

agreed.text: Starch and cellulose are both chains of glucose rings.
agreed.evidence: When either one is broken down completely with acid, the only sugar that comes out is glucose.

agreed.text: Petroleum, natural gas and coal formed from living things buried long ago.
agreed.evidence: Coal holds the prints of leaves and bark. Oil holds molecules that are only made by living cells.

agreed.text: Carbon atoms are made in stars.
agreed.evidence: The light of old stars shows carbon in their outer layers. The high-energy state of carbon that Fred Hoyle predicted in 1953 was found in a laboratory the same year.

challenging.claim: The substances of living things can be made only by living things, because they need a life force.
challenging.who: Most chemists before 1828, including the great Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius.
challenging.for: Nobody had ever made sugar, fat or urea in a laboratory. Substances from living things also burned and charred, while minerals did not.
challenging.against: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from a mineral salt. In 1845 Hermann Kolbe made the acid of vinegar starting from carbon itself. No life force was needed.

challenging.claim: Organic means natural and free of chemicals.
challenging.who: Food labels, shops and everyday speech.
challenging.for: On a food label, organic has a real meaning. It means the crop was grown without factory-made pesticides and fertilisers.
challenging.against: In chemistry, organic means built on carbon chains. Petrol and plastic are organic in this sense. Everything is made of chemicals, including water, mangoes and you. The word has two meanings.

challenging.claim: Coal and oil come from dead dinosaurs.
challenging.who: A common belief, helped by cartoons and toy packets.
challenging.for: Coal and oil are called fossil fuels, and dinosaurs are the best-known fossils.
challenging.against: Most coal formed from swamp forests about 300 million years ago, before the first dinosaurs. Oil formed mostly from tiny sea plants and other sea creatures that sank into mud.

challenging.claim: Plastic has nothing in common with wood, cotton or food.
challenging.for: Plastic is made in factories from petroleum. Plastic does not rot, and no person can live by eating plastic.
challenging.against: Plastic, wood, cotton and food are all built on carbon chains, and the carbon in petroleum came from living things. The real difference is that few microbes have an enzyme that cuts plastic chains. In 2016 scientists in Japan found a bacterium who eats one kind of plastic.

challenging.claim: Somewhere, life could be built on silicon in place of carbon.
challenging.who: Some astrobiologists and many writers of science fiction.
challenging.for: A silicon atom makes four bonds, like a carbon atom. There is far more silicon than carbon in the rocks of the Earth.
challenging.against: Silicon chains break easily and form far fewer shapes. Even on the Earth, with all that silicon, life chose carbon. No silicon life has been found.

big_questions.q: A diamond and the black on a burnt roti are the same element. What makes them so different?
big_questions.hint: Think about the same bricks built into a wall and thrown in a heap.

big_questions.q: Five carbon atoms and twelve hydrogen atoms can make three different liquids. Where is the difference kept?
big_questions.hint: Nothing was added or taken away. Only the pattern of the joins changed.

big_questions.q: A carbon atom in your hand may once have been in a tree, a fish or a dinosaur. Is that atom yours?
big_questions.hint: You will breathe that atom out one day, and a leaf may take that atom in.

big_questions.q: Sugar from a sugarcane and sugar made in a laboratory have the same molecules. Is one more natural than the other?
big_questions.hint: Could any test tell the two apart? If not, what does 'natural' mean here?

big_questions.q: Plastic is made from carbon that living things gathered millions of years ago. Why can living things not take it back?
big_questions.hint: Microbes have enzymes that fit the old chains of wood and food, the way a key fits a lock. Plastic chains are new, so almost no microbe has an enzyme that fits them.

big_questions.q: Burning petrol puts very old carbon into today's air. Who should decide how much we burn?
big_questions.hint: The air is shared by people in every country and by other animals and plants. Children not yet born will share it too.

story.title: The Pot That Came Out Red
story.note: Thenmozhi, Kathir and Paati are made up, and so is this firing. These facts are real. Keeladi is a village near Madurai in Tamil Nadu. Archaeologists have dug up a town there that is more than 2,000 years old. Among the finds are bowls that are black inside and red outside, called black-and-red ware. Manamadurai, further down the Vaigai river, is a potters' town. Many archaeologists think such bowls were fired upside down, with plant matter packed inside. Where air could not reach, carbon from the smoke stayed in the clay. The iron in the clay also turned dark there. Where air could reach, the clay turned red.
text: The bowl in the glass case at Keeladi was broken, and Thenmozhi could not stop looking at it.

It was red on the outside, like any pot in her grandmother's yard. But the inside was black, and so was a band around the rim. The black shone. The card beside it said the bowl was more than two thousand years old.
"Who painted the inside?" asked her cousin Kathir, who was six.
"Nobody," said Thenmozhi. "Paint would have washed off in two thousand years." She did not know how the black had got there. She only knew that she wanted to make one.
Paati's house in Manamadurai had a potter's wheel in the front room and a firing pit behind. Paati had made pots for fifty years. She gave Thenmozhi a lump of clay and asked no questions.

Thenmozhi pinched the clay into a small bowl and dried it for four days in the shade. On firing day Paati set it among her own pots. She packed straw and paddy husk around them and lit the heap in the evening. In the morning Thenmozhi lifted her bowl out with two sticks.
It was red. It was red inside and outside, from rim to foot.
"The fire makes clay red," said Paati. "It has always done so."
"Then I will put the black in myself," said Thenmozhi.

She made a second bowl. When it was dry she held a steel plate over the kitchen lamp until soot gathered on it. She rubbed the soot all over the inside of the bowl with her thumb. It went in black as night. Kathir clapped.
After the next firing, the second bowl was as red as the first. Not one grain of soot was left.
"Where did the soot go?" said Kathir. "Did the fire eat it?"

Thenmozhi had no answer. She sat down beside the firing pit with her chin on her knees. The heap had burnt down in the night. On top lay husk that had turned to soft ash, pale grey, almost white. It fell to powder when she touched it.
She pushed a stick into the heap, only to have something to do. The stick went down a hand's depth and turned up something dark.

She dug with both hands. Under the pale ash, where the husk had been packed tight against the ground, the husk was black. Every piece still had the shape of a husk. It was light and dry, and it left a black line across her palm.
She held white ash in one hand and black husk in the other.
"Same husk," she said slowly. "Same fire. Same night."
"The top got more fire," said Kathir.

"The top got more air," said Thenmozhi. She was thinking of the lamp. A lamp in the wind burned clean, but a lamp under a plate left soot. "On top, the black met the air and burnt away. Down here no air could reach it. So the black stayed."
She looked at her two red bowls. Their insides had been open to the air all night. Any black that touched them had burnt away, soot and all.
"Paati," she called. "Which way up did the old potters put their bowls?"
Paati was wedging clay and did not look up. But she was smiling. "Which way would you put them?"

The third bowl took four more days to dry. On firing day Thenmozhi filled it to the brim with paddy husk. She laid a bed of husk in the pit, turned the bowl over on to the bed and pressed down. Now the inside was shut in with the husk, and no air could get to it. The outside stood open to the fire.
"You are baking it upside down," said Kathir. "All the husk will fall out."
"The husk has nowhere to fall," said Thenmozhi. "And the air has no way in."
The fire burnt through the evening. Thenmozhi slept badly.
In the morning she lifted the bowl with the two sticks and turned it over. Black husk spilled out, each piece still husk-shaped.

The outside of the bowl was red. The inside was black, a deep, even black. A black band ran around the rim, exactly as wide as the part that had sat in the husk bed. She rubbed it with a cloth, and it began to shine.
Kathir put his whole hand inside and pulled it out clean. "It does not come off," he said.
"It is in the clay now," said Thenmozhi.
Paati turned the bowl in her hands for a long time. "My grandmother fired her lamp bowls this way," she said. "I could have told you on the first day. But then it would have been my bowl."
At breakfast, Kathir's dosa came off the tawa with one black edge. He held it up and looked at it. Then he looked at the black bowl on the shelf.
"Is it the same black?" he asked.
"Rice grew, and husk grew," said Thenmozhi. "I think the black is inside everything that grew. We only see it when the heat gets in and the air does not."
story.epiphany: The husk on top of the heap had air, and it burnt away to pale ash. The husk underneath had no air, and it stayed black. Things that grew hold carbon. Heat leaves that carbon behind as a black solid wherever air cannot reach it. In air, the carbon burns and goes into the air as a gas.
ask: The husk on top and the husk underneath were in the same fire. Why did one turn to pale ash and the other stay black?
The soot rubbed inside the second bowl was gone after the firing. Where had the carbon gone?
Kathir asked whether the black on his dosa was the same black as in the bowl. What would you tell him, and how could you test it?

games.title: Chain Line: put the carbon chains in order
games.context: This is a card game about fuels and other carbon chains. Each card describes one substance. You place it in a line, from the shortest carbon chain to the longest.

setup.art: Twelve cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with three cards dealt to each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. Shuffle them. Deal 3 to each player and put the rest in a pile.
