printables.title: 12 chain cards: the substance on the front, the number of carbon atoms on the back

items.f: Methane. The main gas in piped cooking gas and in biogas. It is a gas even in the coldest winter.
items.b: 1 carbon atom. Methane boils at 162 degrees below zero.

items.f: Ethane. A small part of the gas that comes from gas wells.
items.b: 2 carbon atoms. Ethane is a gas. Factories turn it into ethene, to make polythene.

items.f: Propane. One of the two gases in the LPG cylinder.
items.b: 3 carbon atoms. Propane is a gas. Squeezed in a cylinder, it becomes a liquid.

items.f: Butane. The other gas in the LPG cylinder, and the fuel in a gas lighter.
items.b: 4 carbon atoms. Butane boils at 1 degree below zero, so it is a gas in the room.

items.f: Pentane. The lightest liquid in petrol. It dries off your hand in seconds.
items.b: 5 carbon atoms. Pentane is a liquid that boils at 36 degrees.

items.f: Octane. A liquid in petrol that flows as easily as water.
items.b: 8 carbon atoms. Octane is a thin liquid that boils at 126 degrees.

items.f: A kerosene molecule. Kerosene burns in a wick lamp and in jet engines.
items.b: About 12 carbon atoms. Kerosene is a liquid that dries slowly.

items.f: A diesel molecule. Diesel is the oily fuel of lorries, buses and tractors.
items.b: About 16 carbon atoms. Diesel is an oily liquid.

items.f: A fat chain in groundnut oil. The oil is a thick liquid that does not dry.
items.b: 18 carbon atoms in each chain. Each oil molecule has three such chains.

items.f: A candle wax molecule. Wax is a soft solid that melts near a flame.
items.b: About 25 carbon atoms. Wax is a solid in the room.

items.f: A molecule in road tar. Tar is black, sticky and almost solid.
items.b: Often 50 carbon atoms or more, in chains and rings.

items.f: A polythene molecule in a milk packet. Polythene is a tough solid.
items.b: Many thousands of carbon atoms in one chain.

rules: Shuffle the 12 cards, fronts up. Deal 3 to each player and put the rest in a pile. Nobody looks at the backs.
Take the top card of the pile and lay it in the middle, back up. This starts the line.
On your turn, choose a card from your hand and read the front aloud. Put it in the line where you think it belongs. Shorter chains go to the left and longer chains to the right.
Turn your card over. If it is in the right place, it stays, and your turn ends.
If it is in the wrong place, move it to the right place. Then take a new card from the pile.
The first player with no cards left wins.
Playing alone? Start the line with one card. Place the other 11 one at a time. Your score is the number you place correctly at the first try.

flow.do: Cut out the 12 cards. Shuffle them with the fronts up and deal. Start the line with one card, back up.
flow.say: Each card describes one substance built on a carbon chain. The back gives the number of carbon atoms. The line will run from the shortest chain to the longest.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle and deal. Turn one card over to start the line.
flow.context: This is the first step of Chain Line. You set up the cards and start the line.

flow.do: Play by the rules until one player has no cards. When a card is turned over, the player says if the substance is a gas, a liquid or a solid.
flow.say: Read the front before you place your card. Is it a gas, a liquid or a solid? Is it thin or thick? Use that to decide where it goes.
flow.kid: Read your card. Is it a gas, a liquid or a solid? Place it in the line.
flow.parent: If a player is stuck, ask whether the substance is runnier or thicker than the cards already in the line.
flow.context: In this step of Chain Line you take turns placing cards in order of chain length.

flow.do: When the game ends, place any cards still in hands. Read the whole line from left to right. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Read the line from the shortest chain to the longest. Say gas, liquid or solid for each. What happens as the chain gets longer?
flow.kid: Read the line from left to right. What changes as the chain gets longer?

check.q: What happens to carbon-chain fuels as the chain gets longer?
options: They go from gas to liquid to solid
They go from solid to liquid to gas
check.why: Long chains hold on to each other along their whole length. So they are harder to pull apart, and the substance is thicker and boils at a higher temperature.

flow.parent: Chains of 1 to 4 carbon atoms are gases. From about 5 to 18 they are liquids that get thicker. Longer chains are solids.
flow.context: This is the last step of Chain Line. You read the finished line and look for a pattern.

games.title: Carbon Trail: follow one carbon atom
games.context: This is a dice game. You are one carbon atom. The dice send you from the air into leaves, bodies, soil, rock and plastic, and you record where you go.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with eight boxes drawn in a ring, labelled Air, Leaf, Plant body, Animal body, Soil, Deep underground, Plastic and Sea, with a button in the Air box.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 8 boxes on a sheet and write one place in each. Every player puts a token on Air.

setup.art: A child rolling a die beside the sheet and reading a rule card for the place where her token stands.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die. Read what happens at your place for that number. Move your token.

setup.art: A score sheet with a column of twelve numbered lines, the first few filled in with the words Air, Leaf, Animal body, Air.
setup.caption: 3. Write each place on your score sheet. Play 12 rolls.

printables.title: 8 place cards for the board: what each roll of the die does
items: AIR. You are in a molecule of carbon dioxide gas. Roll 1, 2, 3 or 4: a leaf takes you in. Go to Leaf. Roll 5 or 6: you dissolve in sea water. Go to Sea.

LEAF. The leaf has built you into a glucose ring. Roll 1, 2 or 3: the plant joins you into starch or cellulose. Go to Plant body. Roll 4 or 5: the plant uses the glucose for energy and gives you out. Go to Air. Roll 6: a caterpillar eats the leaf. Go to Animal body.

PLANT BODY. You are in wood, cotton or a grain of rice. Roll 1 or 2: an animal eats you. Go to Animal body. Roll 3 or 4: the plant dies and falls. Go to Soil. Roll 5: the wood is burnt. Go to Air. Roll 6: a swamp buries you for millions of years. Go to Deep underground.

ANIMAL BODY. You are in an animal, who may be a child. Roll 1, 2, 3 or 4: the animal uses you for energy and breathes you out. Go to Air. Roll 5: you leave in dung, or the animal dies. Go to Soil. Roll 6: you are built into muscle or bone. Stay here.

SOIL. You are in a dead leaf or in dung. Roll 1, 2, 3 or 4: microbes eat you and breathe you out. Go to Air. Roll 5: you stay in the soil. Roll 6: you are buried deeper and deeper. Go to Deep underground.

DEEP UNDERGROUND. You are in coal, oil or gas. Roll 1, 2, 3 or 6: nothing happens for millions of years. Stay here. Roll 4: people pump you up and burn you as fuel. Go to Air. Roll 5: people pump you up and make plastic. Go to Plastic.

PLASTIC. You are in a long chain in a bottle or a bag. Roll 1, 2, 3 or 4: no microbe can cut your chain. Stay here. Roll 5: the plastic is burnt. Go to Air. Roll 6: the plastic is recycled into a new thing. Stay here.
SEA. You are dissolved in sea water. Roll 1 or 2: you leave the water. Go to Air. Roll 3 or 4: a tiny sea plant takes you in. Go to Leaf. Roll 5 or 6: a sea animal builds you into a shell. Stay here.

printables.title: Carbon Trail score sheet
items: Rolls 1 to 12: write the place you are in after each roll
Longest stay in one place, in rolls

rules: Draw the 8 places as boxes on a sheet of paper. Every player is one carbon atom and starts with a token on Air.
On your turn, roll the die. Read the place card for the place where you are, and do what it says for your number.
Write the place you are in on your score sheet, even if you stayed.
The winner is the player who visited the most different places. If two players tie, the one with the longest stay in one place wins.
Playing alone? Play 12 rolls and count your places. Then play again and try to visit more.

flow.do: Draw the 8 boxes on a sheet of paper and cut out the place cards. Give each player a token and a score sheet. Ask the question below before the first roll.
flow.say: You are one carbon atom, and you start in the air as carbon dioxide. Where do you think you will spend the most time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You are one carbon atom in the air. Where will you stay longest? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Carbon Trail. You set up the board and guess where a carbon atom spends the most time.

flow.do: Play 12 rolls each. After each roll, the player reads the place card aloud and writes the new place on the score sheet.
flow.say: Roll, read your place card aloud and move. Write down where you are after every roll, even if you stayed.
flow.kid: Roll the die. Read your place card. Move, and write where you are.
flow.parent: A player may get stuck underground or in plastic for many rolls. That is the point of those cards, so do not change the rule.
flow.context: In this step of Carbon Trail you roll the die 12 times and record every place your carbon atom visits.

flow.do: Count each player's different places and longest stay. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Count your places and find your longest stay. Which places let you go quickly? Which places held you for a long time?
flow.kid: Count your places. Where did you stay longest? Which places let you go fast?

check.q: Carbon deep underground stays there for millions of years. What moves it quickly into the air?
options: People burning coal, oil and gas
check.why: Left alone, coal and oil stay buried. People dig them up and burn them, which sends very old carbon into the air within a few years. That extra carbon dioxide traps heat.

flow.parent: In the real world a carbon atom spends a few years in the air. In a living body it may stay for days or for centuries. It can spend millions of years in rock or in the deep sea.
flow.context: This is the last step of Carbon Trail. You compare the trails and find which places hold carbon the longest.

experiments.title: The Black Inside: which kitchen things turn black when heated?
experiments.question: Eight small things are heated side by side on a hot tawa for 8 minutes. Which ones turn black, and which ones do not? What do the ones that turn black have in common?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess for each of the eight things: will it turn black, or not? Then say what you think the black ones will have in common. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same small amount of each thing, about as much as one grain of chana. Put all eight on the same tawa, so they get the same heat for the same time. Keep the flame low to medium and do not change it. Look at 3 minutes and again at 8 minutes. Only one thing changes from heap to heap: what the heap is made of.
results_table: Does it leave a black mark on paper?

materials.item: an old tawa or an old steel plate that may get marked
aluminium foil, a piece big enough to cover the tawa
sugar, atta, table salt and baking soda, a small pinch of each
white cotton thread, a piece 3 centimetres long
plain white paper, a square 2 centimetres wide
dry outer skin of an onion, a piece 2 centimetres wide
a steel coin, such as a one-rupee coin
tongs, a steel spoon, a sheet of white paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the heating and stays at the stove. Switch on the exhaust fan or open a window, because the sugar and the paper make smoke. Use only a tiny pinch of each thing. Salt may crackle and jump, so keep faces away. If the paper or thread starts to glow, press it flat with the spoon. Let everything cool for 5 minutes before anyone touches it.
experiments.record: Make a table with eight rows, one for each thing. Write where each thing comes from and its colour after 3 minutes and after 8 minutes. Write whether it leaves a black mark on paper.
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up heats eight kitchen things on a tawa. You find out which ones turn black and what those have in common.

setup.art: A tawa covered with a sheet of foil, with eight tiny heaps in two rows of four, and a paper map beside it naming each heap.
setup.caption: 1. Cover a cold tawa with foil. Put eight tiny heaps on it in two rows. Lay a name slip for each heap beside the tawa in the same rows.

setup.art: A grown-up at a gas stove with a low flame under the tawa, and a child standing one step back, pointing at a heap that has turned brown.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up heats the tawa on a low to medium flame. Look after 3 minutes and write the colours.

setup.art: The same tawa after heating: five heaps are black and three are unchanged, a white heap of salt, a white heap of baking soda and a coin.
setup.caption: 3. Look again after 8 minutes. Then switch off the flame and wait 5 minutes.

setup.art: A child's finger rubbing a black crumb across a sheet of white paper, leaving a black line.
setup.caption: 4. When everything is cool, rub each heap on white paper. Which ones leave a black mark?

flow.do: Lay the eight things on the table. Ask your child to guess for each one, and to give a reason. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will heat these eight things on the tawa for 8 minutes. Which ones do you think will turn black? What will the black ones have in common? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the eight things. Which will turn black? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What do you think the black ones will have in common?
good: They are all food.
They all come from plants.
They are all things that can burn.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say that everything burns black. Others say that white things stay white.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Black Inside. You guess which of eight kitchen things will turn black when heated.

flow.do: Cover the cold tawa with foil. Help your child put a tiny heap of each thing on the foil. Make two rows of four, with gaps between. Write each thing's name on a paper slip. Lay the slips beside the tawa in the same two rows.
flow.say: Each heap must be tiny, about as big as one grain of chana. Why should all the heaps be the same size? Now lay the name slips in the same order, because the heaps will soon look alike.
flow.kid: Put eight tiny heaps on the foil. Keep gaps between them. Lay a name slip for each heap.
flow.parent: Small heaps heat through quickly and make little smoke. Equal heaps keep the test fair. The foil keeps burnt sugar off your tawa.
flow.context: In this step of The Black Inside you set out eight tiny heaps on a foil-covered tawa. You also draw a map of them.

flow.do: Switch on the exhaust fan. Put the tawa on a low to medium flame. Your child stands one step back and watches. At 3 minutes, say the colour of each heap and write it down. At 8 minutes, do the same. Then switch off the flame.
flow.say: Watch each heap and tell me what you see. Which one changed first? Is anything rising from it? I will write the colours at 3 minutes and at 8 minutes.
flow.kid: Stand back and watch. Say what each heap does. A grown-up writes the colours.

check.q: Why are all eight heaps heated together on one tawa?
options: So each heap gets the same heat and time
check.why: On one tawa, every heap gets the same heat for the same time. Then any difference comes from what the heap is made of. If you chose speed or mixing, remember that a fair test changes only one thing.

flow.parent: Sugar usually melts within 2 minutes, turns brown and then black. Thread, paper and onion skin go brown and then black. Atta goes dark brown and may need the full 8 minutes. Salt may crackle. The coin may get a faint yellow or blue tint, but it does not turn into black crumbs. If little has happened by 5 minutes, raise the flame slightly.
flow.context: In this step of The Black Inside a grown-up heats the eight heaps for 8 minutes. You record the colours.

flow.do: Wait 5 minutes for the tawa to cool. Lift the foil on to the table. Your child rubs each heap in turn across white paper with a finger or the spoon. Write yes or no for a black mark.
flow.say: Everything is cool now. Rub each heap across the white paper. Which ones leave a black mark, like a pencil or a piece of charcoal?
flow.kid: Rub each cool heap on white paper. Which ones leave a black mark?
flow.context: In this step of The Black Inside you rub each cooled heap on white paper. You see which ones leave a black mark.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Fill in where each thing comes from. Then read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Now look at where each thing comes from.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What do the things that turned black have in common?
good: They all came from plants.
They were all made by living things.
They all have carbon in them.

ask.q: The sugar was white. Where was the black before you heated it?
good: It was inside the sugar, joined to other things.
It was there but it did not look black.

flow.parent: The five that turned black were all made by plants. Their molecules are chains and rings of carbon atoms, with hydrogen and oxygen atoms attached. Heat drives the hydrogen and oxygen out as water vapour and smoke. A black solid that is mostly carbon stays behind. Salt holds no carbon. Baking soda does hold carbon, but each carbon atom sits alone and leaves as carbon dioxide gas. Write down what you really saw, even if one heap only went brown.
flow.think: Milk is white, and it leaves a black crust when it boils dry. What does that tell you about milk?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Black Inside. You say which things turned black and what they have in common.

experiments.title: One Ring, Three Materials: glucose, cornflour and cotton
experiments.question: Glucose, cornflour and cotton are all built from the same small ring of atoms. Do they behave the same way in cold water, on the tongue and in hot water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. All three are built from one and the same ring. Which will dissolve in cold water? Which will taste sweet? Which will change in hot water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use 2 level teaspoons of each material, or a ball of cotton about that size. Use 100 millilitres of water each time, which is half a small tumbler. Stir each tumbler for 1 minute. Heat each one for 3 minutes on the same low flame. Only one thing changes: the material.
results_table: In cold water after 1 minute of stirring

materials.item: glucose powder, 2 level teaspoons (or table sugar if you have no glucose)
cornflour, 2 level teaspoons (or rice flour or maida)
clean cotton wool, a ball as big as a small lemon
small steel or glass tumblers
drinking water, 300 millilitres
a teaspoon, a small pan and a stove

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the heating. The cornflour paste holds heat, so let it cool before anyone touches it. Taste only a tiny pinch. Do not swallow the cotton.
experiments.record: Make a table with three rows: glucose, cornflour and cotton. For each one, write what happened in cold water, how it tasted, and what happened when it was heated.
experiments.context: In this experiment you test glucose, cornflour and cotton in cold water, on your tongue and in hot water. All three are built from the same ring of atoms. You will find out why one ring can make a sweet powder, a starch and a cloth thread.

setup.art: Three tumblers of water in a row, with a spoon of white powder, a spoon of white flour and a ball of cotton wool lying in front of them.
setup.caption: 1. Pour 100 millilitres of water into each tumbler. Add one material to each. Stir each for 1 minute.

setup.art: The three tumblers after stirring: one clear, one milky white, and one with a wet ball of cotton in clear water.
setup.caption: 2. Look at each tumbler. Is the water clear or cloudy? Can you still see the material?

setup.art: A child touching a pinch of white powder to the tip of her tongue.
setup.caption: 3. Taste a tiny pinch of each dry material. Hold a clean wisp of cotton on your tongue, then take it out.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring a small pan on a stove, with the liquid inside turning thick and glossy.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up heats each tumbler's contents for 3 minutes, stirring. Which one changes?

flow.do: Put the three materials on the table. Tell your child that all three are built from the same small ring, called glucose. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: These three are built from the same ring of atoms, called glucose. In glucose powder the rings are single. In cornflour and cotton they are joined in long chains. Will they behave the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: All three are built from one ring. Will they behave the same? Why?

ask.q: Which one do you think will taste sweet, and why?
good: Glucose, because it is a sugar.
All three, if they are made of the same ring.
Only the powder, because cotton is not food.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good start. Do not say yet which chain is which.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Ring, Three Materials. You guess how glucose, cornflour and cotton will behave in water.

flow.do: Pour 100 millilitres of water into each tumbler. Add 2 level teaspoons of glucose to the first and 2 of cornflour to the second. Put the cotton ball in the third. Your child stirs each for 1 minute, then looks.
flow.say: Stir each one for a slow count of sixty. Now look through the water. Which material can you still see? Wait two minutes and look at the cornflour again.
flow.kid: Stir each tumbler for one minute. Which material can you still see?
flow.parent: The glucose dissolves and the water turns clear. The cornflour makes the water milky, and a white layer settles within a few minutes. The cotton gets wet and stays a ball.
flow.context: In this step of One Ring, Three Materials you stir glucose, cornflour and cotton into cold water and compare them.

flow.do: Your child tastes a tiny pinch of dry glucose, then a tiny pinch of dry cornflour. Then they hold a clean wisp of cotton on the tongue for a moment and take it out. Write the tastes.
flow.say: Taste a tiny pinch of each powder. Then hold this clean wisp of cotton on your tongue and take it out again. Which ones taste sweet?
flow.kid: Taste a pinch of each powder. Touch the cotton to your tongue. Which is sweet?

check.q: Cornflour is made of glucose rings. Why does it not taste sweet?
options: Its rings are joined in long chains
It has no rings in it
It is too cold to taste
check.why: The sweet sensors on your tongue fit small sugar molecules. A starch chain is far too big to fit. If you chose 'no rings', remember that starch is built from the same glucose rings.

flow.context: In this step of One Ring, Three Materials you taste glucose and cornflour, and touch cotton to your tongue.

flow.do: Heat the glucose water in the small pan on a low flame for 3 minutes, stirring. Pour it back. Do the same with the cotton and its water. Stir the cornflour water well, then heat it last. Your child watches from one step back.
flow.say: I will heat each one for 3 minutes. Watch the spoon as I stir. Tell me the moment anything changes.
flow.kid: Watch the pan from one step back. Which one changes when heated?
flow.parent: The glucose water stays thin. The cotton does not change. The cornflour water turns thick and glossy quite suddenly, just before it boils. Heat the cornflour last, because it leaves the pan sticky.
flow.context: In this step of One Ring, Three Materials a grown-up heats each tumbler's contents for 3 minutes.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Then read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The ring is the same in all three. What is different?
good: How many rings are joined.
The way the rings are joined.
One is single rings and two are long chains.

flow.parent: Glucose is single rings. They are small, so water molecules surround each one and carry it off. That is dissolving. They also fit the sweet sensors on the tongue. Starch is a coiled chain of hundreds or thousands of rings, packed into tiny grains. The grains are too big to dissolve in cold water. Hot water gets in between the chains, the grains swell and burst, and the loose chains tangle. That thickens the water. Cellulose is a straight chain in which every second ring is turned over. Straight chains lie side by side and hold each other tightly, so water cannot separate them.
flow.think: A cotton shirt is washed in water hundreds of times and does not dissolve. What would happen if cotton were single rings?
flow.context: This is the last step of One Ring, Three Materials. You say why three materials built from one ring behave so differently.

experiments.title: Foil Packet Charcoal: what is left when wood is heated without air?
experiments.question: One wooden toothpick is burnt in the open flame. Ten more are heated in the same flame, wrapped tightly in foil so that almost no air can reach them. What is left in each case?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What will be left of the toothpick burnt in the open? What will be inside the foil packet: ash, wood that looks the same, or something else? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use toothpicks from the same box. Heat both in the same flame. Only one thing changes: whether air can reach the wood.

materials.item: wooden toothpicks from one box (or matchsticks with the heads cut off)
aluminium foil, two pieces about 20 centimetres square
a pin
long tongs and a gas stove
a steel plate and a sheet of white paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the heating, with tongs, and the child stands one step back. Switch on the exhaust fan, because white smoke comes out of the pinhole. The smoke may catch fire in a small flame, which is expected. Leave the packet closed on the steel plate for 10 minutes. If it is opened hot, the charcoal can start to glow and burn.
experiments.record: Make a table with two rows: the toothpick burnt in the open, and the toothpicks in the foil packet. Write what was left, its colour, whether it kept its shape and whether it draws on paper.
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up heats wooden toothpicks in the open flame and inside a tight foil packet. You compare what is left.

setup.art: Ten wooden toothpicks lying side by side on a square of foil, with a second square of foil and a pin beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 10 toothpicks on the foil. Wrap them tightly in two layers. Fold each edge over three times.

setup.art: A flat foil packet with one small pinhole in the top, and a hand holding a pin above it.
setup.caption: 2. Prick one pinhole in the packet. This lets the smoke out.

setup.art: A grown-up holding one toothpick in tongs in a gas flame, with the toothpick burning with a yellow flame.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up burns one toothpick in the open flame. Look at what is left.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the foil packet in tongs in a gas flame, with a thin line of white smoke coming from the pinhole.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up heats the packet until the smoke stops, about 5 to 8 minutes. Leave it closed for 10 minutes.

setup.art: An opened foil packet showing ten thin black sticks, and a child drawing a black line on paper with one of them.
setup.caption: 5. Open the cool packet. Count the sticks. Try to draw with one.

flow.do: Show the toothpicks and the foil. Explain the two cases. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: One toothpick will burn in the open flame. Ten will be heated inside foil, where almost no air can reach them. What will be left each time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One stick burns in air. Ten are heated in foil. What will be left? Why?

ask.q: Why might the foil make a difference?
good: Fire needs air.
The foil keeps the flame away from the wood.
The smoke cannot get out.

flow.parent: Many children expect ash in both cases. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Foil Packet Charcoal. You guess what is left when wood is heated with air and without air.

flow.do: Your child lays 10 toothpicks side by side on one foil square and wraps them tightly. Wrap the second square around the first. Fold each edge over three times and press flat. Your child pricks one pinhole in the top.
flow.say: Wrap the sticks as tightly as you can, so that very little air stays inside. Now make one small hole with the pin. What do you think the hole is for?
flow.kid: Wrap ten sticks tightly in foil, twice. Prick one hole with the pin.
flow.parent: Heated wood gives off gases. The pinhole lets them out, so the packet does not puff open. Very little air gets in through so small a hole while gas is rushing out.
flow.context: In this step of Foil Packet Charcoal you wrap ten toothpicks tightly in two layers of foil. Then you prick one pinhole.

flow.do: Hold one toothpick in the tongs in the gas flame until nothing more burns or glows. Tip what is left on to the steel plate. Your child looks and writes.
flow.say: Watch this one stick in the open flame. It has all the air it needs. What is left at the end? Touch it once the plate is cool.
flow.kid: Watch one stick burn in the flame. Look at what is left.
flow.parent: The stick burns with a flame, then glows, then leaves a tiny speck of pale grey ash. Often the ash is so light that it floats away.
flow.context: In this step of Foil Packet Charcoal a grown-up burns one toothpick in the open flame. You look at what is left.

flow.do: Hold the packet in the tongs in the flame, pinhole upward. Turn it over once a minute. White smoke comes from the hole after about a minute. Keep heating until the smoke stops, about 5 to 8 minutes. Put the packet on the steel plate and leave it closed for 10 minutes.
flow.say: Watch the pinhole. Something is coming out of the wood. What do you think it is? When the smoke stops, I will put the packet down to cool.
flow.kid: Watch the pinhole from one step back. What comes out? Wait until it cools.

check.q: Why must the foil packet stay closed until it is cool?
options: Hot charcoal burns away when air reaches it
check.why: Hot carbon joins with the oxygen in air and burns. Kept closed, it cools with no air and stays as charcoal. If you chose the smoke, remember that the smoke had already left.

flow.parent: The smoke may light with a small flame at the hole. That is the wood gas burning, and it is safe at the stove. Use the 10 minutes of cooling for the cards or the story.
flow.context: In this step of Foil Packet Charcoal a grown-up heats the foil packet until the smoke stops. Then the packet cools for 10 minutes.

flow.do: Open the cool packet on the plate. Your child counts the sticks, snaps one and draws with another. Ask them to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why. Then read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Count the sticks. Snap one and draw with one. Now say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Count the sticks. Draw with one. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: Both lots of wood were in the same flame. Why is one ash and the other black sticks?
good: The sticks in the foil had no air, so they could not burn.
The carbon stayed because it could not join with oxygen.

ask.q: What was the smoke from the pinhole made of?
good: The other parts of the wood, leaving as gas.
Water and gases from the wood.

flow.parent: Wood is built of carbon chains and rings, with hydrogen and oxygen atoms attached. Heat breaks them up. The hydrogen and oxygen leave as water vapour and smoky gases, and they carry some of the carbon away too. Inside the foil there is no air, so the rest of the carbon cannot burn. It stays as charcoal, in the shape of the stick. In the open, the carbon joins with oxygen and leaves as carbon dioxide gas. Only a speck of minerals is left as ash. If the sticks are still brown inside, wrap them again and heat for 3 more minutes.
flow.think: A charcoal stick glows red when lit, but gives almost no flame or smoke. Where did its flame and smoke go?
flow.context: This is the last step of Foil Packet Charcoal. You compare the black sticks from the packet with the ash from the open flame.

activities.title: One Bond or Four: which atom can build the most?

materials.item: small coins, to be atoms that make one bond
medium coins, to be atoms that make two bonds
big coins or bottle caps, to be atoms that make four bonds
matchsticks or toothpicks, to be bonds
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Build molecules with atoms that make one, two or four bonds. Compare how many different molecules each atom can build.

activities.record: Take a photo of your best build from each round, or draw it. Write how many different molecules each kind of atom could build.
activities.context: In this activity coins are atoms and matchsticks are bonds. You build molecules with atoms that make one, two or four bonds. You will find out why carbon can build far more than other atoms.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three circles drawn on it: one with a single line coming out, one with two lines and one with four lines.
setup.caption: 1. Each coin is an atom. Each matchstick is a bond. Small coins make 1 bond, medium coins make 2 bonds, and big coins make 4 bonds.

setup.art: A drawing of two small circles joined by one line, with a tick beside it.
setup.caption: 2. A molecule is finished when every bond joins two atoms and no atom has a bond left over.

setup.art: A drawing of three circles marked C in a row joined by lines, with eight small circles marked H joined around them.
setup.caption: 3. Build with each kind of atom. Count how many different finished molecules you find.

flow.do: Explain the rules below. Then ask the question before any building, and write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: An atom is a coin and a bond is a matchstick. A small coin makes 1 bond, a medium coin makes 2, and a big coin makes 4. Which kind will build the most different molecules? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A small coin makes 1 bond. A medium one makes 2. A big one makes 4. Which builds the most? Why?
flow.parent: The rule for a finished molecule: every line joins two atoms, and every atom has exactly its number of lines.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Bond or Four. You guess which kind of atom can build the most different molecules.

flow.do: Round 1: your child uses only small coins and builds every finished molecule they can. Round 2: they use only medium coins.
flow.say: Use only small coins first. How many different finished molecules can you build? Now use only medium coins. A row has two loose ends. How could you finish it?
flow.kid: Build with small coins only. Then with medium coins only. How many can you finish?

ask.q: Why can one-bond atoms only make a pair?
good: Once two join, neither has a bond left.
There is nothing left to hold a third atom.

flow.parent: One-bond atoms give only a pair. Two-bond atoms give rows, but a row has two loose ends. It is finished only when it closes into a loop. So two-bond atoms make plain loops of different sizes and nothing else. They cannot branch. A child may also join two atoms with two lines. That is allowed, and it is how two oxygen atoms are really joined in oxygen gas.
flow.context: In this step of One Bond or Four you build with atoms that make one bond. Then you build with atoms that make two bonds.

flow.do: Round 3: your child joins big coins in a row and puts a small coin on every spare bond. They build with 1, then 2, then 3 big coins, and count the small coins each time. Then they try 4 big coins in two different patterns.
flow.say: Now use big coins, and put a small coin on each spare bond. Build with one, then two, then three. Count the small coins each time. Then find two different ways to join four.
flow.kid: Join big coins in a row. Put a small coin on each spare bond. Count the small coins.

check.q: A four-bond atom sits in the middle of a chain. How many bonds does it have left over?
check.why: It uses two bonds to hold its two neighbours, so two are left. Each can hold a small atom or start a branch. If you chose none, count again: four take away two.

flow.parent: With one, two and three four-bond atoms, you need 4, 6 and 8 one-bond atoms. Four four-bond atoms can make a straight row, or a row of three with a branch. These molecules are real gases. They are methane, ethane, propane and two kinds of butane.
flow.context: In this step of One Bond or Four you build chains with atoms that make four bonds. You fill the spare bonds with one-bond atoms.

flow.do: Put the three builds side by side. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why. Then tell them which real atoms these are.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. The one-bond atom is hydrogen. The two-bond atom is oxygen. The four-bond atom is carbon.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why.

ask.q: Why can the four-bond atom build so much more?
good: It can hold two neighbours and still have bonds left.
It can make branches.
Its chains can go on as long as you like.

flow.parent: There is one more reason carbon builds so well. The bond between two carbon atoms is strong, so long chains last. Real oxygen atoms hold each other weakly, and long oxygen chains fall apart.
flow.context: This is the last step of One Bond or Four. You compare what atoms with one, two and four bonds could build.

activities.title: Five Carbons: how many different skeletons can you find?

materials.item: coins of the same size, or bottle caps, to be carbon atoms
matchsticks or toothpicks, to be bonds
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Join five coins with matchsticks in every different pattern you can find, and photograph or draw each one.

activities.record: Take a photo of every different skeleton you find for five carbon atoms, or draw each one. Write how many you found.
activities.context: In this activity coins are carbon atoms and matchsticks are bonds. You find every different way to join five carbon atoms.

setup.art: Five coins in a straight row on a table with a matchstick lying between each pair.
setup.caption: 1. Coins are carbon atoms. Matchsticks are bonds. Join 5 coins in a row with 4 matchsticks.

setup.art: Four coins in a row with a fifth coin joined above the second coin by a matchstick.
setup.caption: 2. Move one coin to make a branch. No coin may touch more than 4 matchsticks.

setup.art: A page with three small drawings of five dots joined in different patterns, numbered 1 to 3.
setup.caption: 3. Photograph or draw each new skeleton. Two are the same if you can turn or bend one into the other.

flow.do: Lay out 5 coins in a row with 4 matchsticks between them. Explain the rule for 'the same'. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: These five coins are carbon atoms in a chain. How many different ways can five carbon atoms be joined, with no rings? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Five coins are five carbon atoms. How many ways can you join them? Why?
flow.parent: Two patterns are the same if one can be turned, flipped or bent into the other without lifting a matchstick. A bent row is still a row.
flow.context: This is the first step of Five Carbons. You guess how many different skeletons five carbon atoms can make.

flow.do: Your child moves coins and matchsticks to find new patterns, and photographs or draws each one. All 5 coins must stay joined, with 4 matchsticks and no loops. Check each new one against the rule for 'the same'.
flow.say: Find a new pattern and photograph or draw it. Is it truly new, or is it an old one turned round? Keep going until you are sure there are no more.
flow.kid: Move the coins to find a new pattern. Take a photo or draw it. Is it truly new?

check.q: A row of five coins is bent into an L shape. Is this a new skeleton?
options: No, each coin has the same neighbours
Only if a coin is added
check.why: A skeleton is about which atom is joined to which. Bending changes none of the joins. Real chains bend and wriggle all the time. If you chose yes, check each coin's neighbours before and after.

flow.parent: There are exactly three. One is a straight row of five. One is a row of four with one branch. One is a cross, with one coin in the middle holding four others.
flow.context: In this step of Five Carbons you search for every different way to join five coins with four matchsticks.

flow.do: Look at the drawings together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why. Then tell them about the three real liquids. If there is time, try 6 coins.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Each of your three skeletons is a real liquid, with its own boiling point.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why.

ask.q: All three have 5 carbon atoms and 12 hydrogen atoms. Why are they different substances?
good: The atoms are joined in a different pattern.
The shape of the molecule is different.

flow.parent: The straight chain boils at 36 degrees Celsius, the branched one at 28 and the cross at 10. Substances with the same atoms joined differently are called isomers. Six carbon atoms make 5 skeletons, and ten make 75.
flow.think: If the two ends of the row of five join, you get a ring. Is a ring the same skeleton as a row?
flow.context: This is the last step of Five Carbons. You count the skeletons you found and learn that each one is a real substance.

activities.title: Paper Chain Starch: join eight glucose rings and count the water

materials.item: strips of paper about 15 centimetres long and 2 centimetres wide
glue or sticky tape
chana, rajma or buttons, to be atoms that leave as water
a small bowl

schedule.what: Join eight paper loops into a chain and count one water molecule for every join. Then cut the chain apart again.

activities.record: Write how many rings you joined, how many joins you made and how many water molecules came out.
activities.context: In this activity each paper loop is one glucose ring. You join eight loops into a starch chain and count the water that each join gives off.

setup.art: Eight separate paper loops on a table, each with three chana seeds placed beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Make 8 separate paper loops. Each loop is one glucose ring.

setup.art: Two paper loops being linked, with three seeds being dropped into a small bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Each time you link two loops, put 3 seeds in the bowl. Together they stand for one molecule of water.

setup.art: A chain of eight linked paper loops beside a bowl holding seven little groups of three seeds.
setup.caption: 3. Link all 8. Count the joins and the water molecules.

flow.do: Show one paper loop and say that it stands for one glucose ring. Ask the question and write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: This loop is one glucose ring. A plant joins rings into a long chain called starch. If I join 8 rings in a row, how many joins will there be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One loop is one glucose ring. Eight loops in a chain need how many joins? Why?
flow.parent: Many children say 8. The chain will show them.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper Chain Starch. You guess how many joins hold eight glucose rings in one chain.

flow.do: Your child makes loops from the strips and links them one at a time into a chain. For every join, they drop 3 seeds into the bowl as one molecule of water. They count joins aloud.
flow.say: Each time two rings join, one molecule of water comes out. A water molecule has three atoms, so put three seeds in the bowl. Count each join aloud.
flow.kid: Link the loops one by one. Drop three seeds in the bowl for each join.

check.q: Eight glucose rings join into one chain. How many water molecules come out?
check.why: A row of 8 rings has 7 joins between them, and each join gives off one water molecule. If you chose eight, line up 8 coins and count the gaps between them.

flow.context: In this step of Paper Chain Starch you link eight paper loops and count one water molecule for every join.

flow.do: Now run it backwards. Your child tears the chain apart one join at a time. For each cut, they take 3 seeds back out of the bowl. Ask them to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why.
flow.say: Your body does the opposite when you digest starch. Each cut uses up one water molecule. Take three seeds back for every cut. Then say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why.
flow.kid: Tear the joins one by one. Take three seeds back each time. Say what you found.

ask.q: After all the cuts, how many seeds are left in the bowl?
good: None. Seven waters came out and seven went back in.

flow.parent: Joining gives off water and cutting uses water. This is true for starch, cellulose, proteins and fats. A real starch chain has hundreds or thousands of rings.
flow.context: This is the last step of Paper Chain Starch. You cut the chain back into single rings, as digestion does, and use up the water again.

projects.title: The Carbon Hunt: twenty things you touch in one day

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
things already in your home, with their labels

projects.safety: Do not heat or burn anything for this project. Use labels, your eyes and what you know about where each thing came from.

schedule.what: List 20 things you touch between waking and bedtime, and guess which ones are built on carbon chains.
Sort the 20 things into three groups, count each group and compare with your guess.

projects.record: Make a list of 20 things. Beside each, write what it is made of and one of three groups: carbon chains made by a living being, carbon chains made by people from petroleum, or no carbon chains.
projects.context: In this two-day project you list 20 things you touch in a day. You sort them by whether they are built on carbon chains and where those chains came from.

setup.art: A child in the morning holding a toothbrush, with a notebook open beside the sink showing a numbered list.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1. Write down 20 things you touch, from your toothbrush to your pillow.

setup.art: A child reading the label inside the collar of a shirt, with a plastic bottle turned over to show the triangle mark on its base.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2. Find what each is made of. Read labels on clothes and the marks on plastic.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns headed with a leaf, a factory and a stone, and things listed under each.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the 20 into three groups and count each group.

flow.do: Day 1. Through the day, your child writes down 20 things they touch. In the evening, ask for the guess below and the reason. Write both down.
flow.say: You have listed 20 things. How many of them do you think are built on carbon chains? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: List 20 things you touch today. How many hold carbon chains? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Ask for a mix: clothes, food, furniture, vessels, toys, the floor, a tap, a book. Do not sort them yet.
flow.context: This is day 1 of The Carbon Hunt. You list 20 things you touch in one day and guess how many are built on carbon chains.

flow.do: Day 2. For each thing, your child finds what it is made of. Read clothes labels and the triangle marks on plastic. Then they put it in one of three groups, using the clues in the note below.
flow.say: For each thing, ask two questions. Did a living being make this material? If not, was it made from petroleum? If the answer to both is no, it has no carbon chains.
flow.kid: Find what each thing is made of. Put it in one of three groups.

check.q: A shirt label says '100% polyester'. Which group does the shirt belong to?
options: Carbon chains made by a living being
check.why: Polyester is a plastic thread, made in a factory from petroleum. Its long molecules have a carbon frame. If you chose a living being, you may have thought of cotton, which grows on a plant.

flow.parent: Made by a living being: cotton, wood, paper, food, wool, silk, leather, natural rubber, coir. Made by people from petroleum: plastic, polyester, nylon, acrylic, foam, most paint, most shoe soles. No carbon chains: steel, aluminium, brass, glass, clay, stone, cement, water, salt. Some things belong to two groups, such as a pencil or a steel tumbler with a plastic lid. Count each part.
flow.context: This is day 2 of The Carbon Hunt. You sort your 20 things into three groups by where their material came from.

flow.do: Count the three groups together. Ask your child to say what they thought they would find and what they found. Ask why they think it came out that way.
flow.say: Count each group. Say what you thought you would find, what you found, and why you think it came out that way. Which group surprised you?
flow.kid: Count each group. Say what you guessed and what you found. Say why.

ask.q: What do the things with no carbon chains have in common?
good: They came from rock, sand or metal.
They were never part of a living being.
Most are hard and do not burn.

flow.parent: In most homes, well over half the 20 things are built on carbon chains. The carbon in the petroleum group was also gathered by living beings, millions of years ago.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Carbon Hunt. You count your three groups and compare them with your guess.

challenges.title: The Drawing Stick: make charcoal that draws dark and does not snap
challenges.problem: Artists draw with sticks of charcoal. A good stick draws a dark line and does not snap in the hand. In Foil Packet Charcoal, toothpicks were heated in a tight foil packet and came out as thin black sticks. Those sticks draw, but they snap easily. Your problem is to make a better drawing stick, with the same foil packet method and things from home.
constraints: A grown-up does all the heating, and the packet cools for 10 minutes before it is opened.
Use only wood, paper or cotton that you already have at home.
Test 1: the stick must draw a line 10 centimetres long that is clearly black.
Test 2: the stick must draw five such lines without snapping.
Change only one thing between one packet and the next.
materials: aluminium foil, tongs, a pin and a gas stove, as in Foil Packet Charcoal
wooden things of different thickness: toothpicks, matchsticks with the heads cut off, bamboo skewers, ice-cream sticks
a sheet of newspaper and a length of thick cotton string
white paper and a ruler for the line tests
general: Use thicker wood, such as a piece of bamboo skewer or half an ice-cream stick.
Heat until the smoke from the pinhole has fully stopped, so that no brown wood is left inside.
Let the packet cool completely before opening, so that the stick does not start to burn.
creative: Roll a strip of newspaper into a tight stick as thick as a pencil. Tie it with cotton thread and char the roll.
Char a bundle of three toothpicks tied tightly with thread, so that they come out as one stick.
Wrap paper tape around one end of the finished stick as a holder. It keeps your fingers clean and supports the stick.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own drawing stick. It must pass both tests: one clearly black line of 10 centimetres, and five lines without snapping. Use your best stick to draw a picture or write your name. Write what you changed and which test was harder to pass.
challenges.context: In this challenge you make a charcoal stick for drawing, with the foil packet method. The stick must draw a dark line and must not snap.

setup.art: Toothpicks, a bamboo skewer, an ice-cream stick and a tight roll of newspaper laid in a row beside a square of foil.
setup.caption: 1. Choose what to char. Try wood of different thickness, or tightly rolled paper.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a foil packet in tongs over a gas flame, with a child one step back holding a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up heats the packet until the smoke stops. Let it cool for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A child drawing a line beside a ruler with a black stick, with four more black lines already on the paper.
setup.caption: 3. Test the stick. Draw five lines of 10 centimetres. Is each line black? Did the stick snap?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Your child draws a 10 centimetre line with a toothpick stick from Foil Packet Charcoal, if one is left. Ask what is good and what is poor about it.
flow.say: In Foil Packet Charcoal, the toothpicks came out as thin black sticks. Draw a line with one. What is good about it? What goes wrong?
flow.kid: Draw a line with a thin charcoal stick. What is good? What goes wrong?

ask.q: Why does the thin stick snap so easily?
good: It is very thin.
Charcoal is brittle.
Much of the wood left as smoke.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Drawing Stick. You test a thin charcoal stick and find its faults.

flow.do: Your child chooses one thing to change and says why. Help them wrap the new packet tightly in two layers of foil with one pinhole.
flow.say: Choose one thing to change: the thickness, the material or the heating time. Why do you think your change will help? Wrap the packet tightly.
flow.kid: Choose one thing to change. Say why. Wrap the new packet tightly.
flow.parent: Thicker wood needs longer heating, often 8 to 10 minutes. Keep heating until the smoke stops.
flow.context: In this step of The Drawing Stick you choose one change and wrap a new foil packet.

flow.do: Heat the packet in the flame with tongs until the smoke stops. Put it on a steel plate and leave it closed for 10 minutes. Your child rules five faint pencil lines of 10 centimetres while they wait.
flow.say: I will heat the packet until the smoke stops. Rule five pencil lines of 10 centimetres while the packet cools.
flow.kid: Watch from one step back. Rule five lines while the packet cools.
flow.context: In this step of The Drawing Stick a grown-up heats the new packet, and it cools for 10 minutes.

flow.do: Open the cool packet. Your child runs both tests and writes the results. Talk about the question below. If there is time, change one more thing and try again.
flow.say: Run both tests. Is the line clearly black? Did the stick last for five lines? What would you change next?
flow.kid: Draw five lines. Is each one black? Did the stick snap? What next?

ask.q: Your stick is brown inside and draws a pale line. What went wrong?
good: It was not heated long enough.
The middle is still wood.

flow.parent: Artists' charcoal is made in the same way, from willow or vine twigs heated in a closed kiln. Praise a clear account of what was changed and what happened.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Drawing Stick. You test your new charcoal stick and decide what to change next.

items.p: How many bonds does one carbon atom make?
items.why: A carbon atom makes four bonds. That lets it hold two neighbours in a chain and still have two bonds free.

items.p: Charcoal and diamond are made of the same kind of atom.
items.why: True. Both are carbon. In diamond every atom holds four others in a tight network. In charcoal the atoms are joined in a jumble.

items.p: A substance made of only one kind of atom is called an ____.
items.why: Carbon, oxygen and iron are elements. Sugar is not, because it holds three kinds of atom.

items.p: Sort these by what happens on a hot tawa. Does each one turn black or not?
items.why: Sugar, cotton and paper were made by plants and are built on carbon chains. Salt and steel hold no carbon chains.

items.p: Sugar is white. Why does it turn black when it is heated strongly?
items.why: Heat drives hydrogen and oxygen out of the sugar as water vapour and gases. The carbon atoms stay behind as a black solid.

items.p: Match each fuel to the length of its carbon chain.
items.why: The shortest chains are gases. Longer chains are liquids, and the longest are solids.

items.p: A longer carbon chain makes a fuel thinner and quicker to boil.
items.why: False. Longer chains hold on to each other more strongly. So the fuel is thicker and boils at a higher temperature.

items.p: Rice, potato and cornflour are mostly ____, a long chain of glucose rings.
items.why: Plants join glucose rings into starch and pack the starch away as a food store.

items.p: Which of these is built from glucose rings joined in long, straight chains?
items.why: Cotton is mostly cellulose. Each cellulose molecule is a straight chain of thousands of glucose rings.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest carbon chain to the longest.
items.why: Methane has 1 carbon atom, butane 4, octane 8, wax about 25 and polythene many thousands.

items.p: Salt and sugar are both white grains. Explain why only sugar leaves a black solid when heated.
items.a: Sugar molecules are built on carbon atoms joined in rings, with hydrogen and oxygen attached. Heat drives off the hydrogen and oxygen, and carbon is left. Salt holds no carbon, so nothing black can be left.
items.why: A strong answer says that the black solid is carbon and that it was inside the sugar all along. It says that salt has no carbon.

items.p: Glucose dissolves in cold water, but cotton does not. Both are built from the same ring. Explain the difference.
items.a: Glucose is single small rings, so water can surround each one and carry it away. In cotton the rings are joined in long straight chains that hold each other tightly. Water cannot pull them apart.
items.why: A strong answer says that the ring is the same and the joining is different. It links small molecules to dissolving.

items.p: Draw a chain of 3 carbon atoms. Add hydrogen atoms until every carbon atom has 4 bonds.
items.a: Three C atoms in a row joined by two lines. The two end atoms each hold 3 H atoms, and the middle atom holds 2. That is 8 H atoms in all.
items.why: A strong drawing gives every carbon atom exactly four lines and every hydrogen atom exactly one. This molecule is propane.
items.art: A blank box with the letters C and H shown in a small key at the side.

items.p: Is a plastic bottle 'unnatural'?

views.says: Yes. A factory made the bottle. Nothing in a forest makes plastic, and nothing in a forest can eat it.
No. The bottle is carbon chains, like wood. Its carbon came from sea creatures who lived millions of years ago.
The word does not help much. What matters is whether any living being can take the material apart again.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about carbon chains. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that plastic and wood share a carbon frame. Another is that microbes have enzymes for wood but almost none for plastic.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses a fact about carbon chains or about microbes, and answers another view fairly.

items.p: Where does a plant get the carbon to build wood?
opts: From carbon dioxide in the air
items.why: A leaf takes carbon dioxide from the air and joins the carbon into glucose. Sunlight gives the energy, but light is not a material.

items.p: An atom makes only one bond. What is the biggest molecule that such atoms can build alone?
items.why: Once two one-bond atoms join, neither has a bond left for a third. Hydrogen gas is made of such pairs.

items.p: A carbon atom in the middle of a chain has two bonds left. What can they hold?
items.why: Each spare bond can hold a hydrogen atom, or it can hold another carbon atom and start a branch.

items.p: Baking soda holds carbon, so it turns black on a hot tawa.
items.why: False. Each carbon atom in baking soda sits alone, held by oxygen atoms. When heated, it leaves as carbon dioxide gas. A black solid needs carbon atoms joined to each other.

items.p: Bending a chain of five carbon atoms makes a new substance.
items.why: False. Bending changes no joins. A new substance needs the atoms to be joined in a different pattern, such as a branch.

items.p: A chain of 4 carbon atoms is filled up with hydrogen atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it hold?
items.why: The two end atoms hold 3 each and the two middle atoms hold 2 each. 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10. This is butane.

items.p: Twenty glucose rings join into one chain. How many water molecules come out?
items.why: A chain of 20 rings has 19 joins, and each join gives off one water molecule.

items.p: Three of these are built on carbon chains. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Cotton, polythene and wood are carbon chains. Steel is mostly iron, which came from rock.

items.p: Sort these carbon-chain materials. Who made the chains?
items.why: Silkworms make silk, trees make the fibres of paper and coconut palms make the oil. Nylon, PET and polyester are made in factories from petroleum.

items.p: Match each material to what its molecules are.
items.why: All four are built from sugar rings. They differ in how many rings are joined and in what way.

items.p: Wood heated inside tight foil turns to charcoal. Wood heated in the open turns to ash. Explain why.
items.a: Inside the foil there is no air, so the carbon cannot burn and stays behind as charcoal. In the open, carbon joins with oxygen from the air and leaves as carbon dioxide gas. Only a little mineral ash is left.
items.why: A strong answer names the one difference, which is air. It says where the carbon went in each case.

items.p: Cornflour does not thicken cold water, but it thickens hot water. Explain what the heat does.
items.a: Starch chains are packed into tiny grains that cold water cannot enter. Hot water gets in between the chains. The grains swell and burst, and the loose chains tangle and hold the water.
items.why: A strong answer speaks about long chains in grains, and says the hot water frees them to tangle.

items.p: Many people think coal and oil are made from dinosaurs. What would you tell them, and what evidence would you give?
items.a: Most coal formed from swamp forests, long before the dinosaurs. Oil formed mostly from tiny sea plants and other sea creatures buried in mud. Coal still holds the prints of leaves and bark.
items.why: A strong answer corrects the belief kindly and gives evidence, such as leaf prints in coal.

items.p: Label the three skeletons that five carbon atoms can make.
a: Straight chain: five atoms in one row
Chain with one branch: four in a row, and one joined to the second atom
Cross: one atom in the middle, holding four others
items.why: These are the only three ways to join five carbon atoms without a ring. Each is a real liquid with its own boiling point.
items.art: Three small diagrams of five dots joined by lines: a row of five, a row of four with one dot above the second, and a plus shape, each with a blank label line.

items.p: Should a food packet be allowed to say 'chemical-free'?

views.says: Yes. Customers know what it means. It means nothing was added in a factory.
No. Everything is made of chemicals. Sugar, water and salt are chemicals, so the label cannot be true.

views.who: A farmer who grows without pesticides
views.says: The words are loose, but the difference is real. The label should say exactly what was not used.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer notices that the word 'chemical' is used with two meanings. It may suggest a clearer label.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about words. A strong answer separates what is true in chemistry from what the customer wants to know.

items.p: Fuel gas from a cylinder burns. What becomes of its carbon atoms?
opts: They join oxygen as carbon dioxide
items.why: Atoms are never lost. Each carbon atom joins with oxygen and leaves as carbon dioxide gas. The heat comes from the new bonds forming.

items.p: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from a mineral salt. Which idea did this test?
opts: That only living bodies make such substances
items.why: Chemists thought a life force was needed. Wöhler made a substance of the body from a mineral, with no living thing involved.

items.p: A diamond is burnt in pure oxygen. Only carbon dioxide forms. What does this show?
opts: Diamond is a kind of glass
items.why: Carbon dioxide holds only carbon and oxygen. The oxygen was supplied, so the carbon must have come from the diamond, and nothing else was in it.

items.p: Silicon atoms also make four bonds. Why is life not built on silicon chains?
items.why: Bonds between silicon atoms are weaker than bonds between carbon atoms. Long silicon chains fall apart in water and air. Silicon is not rare: sand is full of it.

items.p: Where were the carbon atoms in your body first made?
items.why: Old stars press three helium atoms into one carbon atom. Dying stars threw that carbon into space, and the Earth formed from it.

items.p: Two substances with exactly the same atoms must behave in exactly the same way.
items.why: False. The three liquids made of 5 carbon and 12 hydrogen atoms boil at 36, 28 and 10 degrees. The pattern of the joins matters too.

items.p: Petrol is an organic substance, in the chemist's meaning of the word.
items.why: True. In chemistry, organic means built on carbon chains. Petrol is carbon chains. On a food label the word has a different meaning.

items.p: About 18 of every 100 kilograms of a body is carbon. How many kilograms of carbon are in a 50 kilogram person?
items.why: 50 is half of 100, so the carbon is half of 18. Half of 18 is 9 kilograms.

items.p: Put the journey of one carbon atom in order, starting in the air.
items: Starch in a grain of rice
Carbon dioxide in the child's breath
a: Starch in a grain of rice
Carbon dioxide in the child's breath
items.why: The leaf takes carbon from the air and builds glucose. The plant stores the glucose as starch. The child digests the starch to glucose, uses it for energy and breathes the carbon out.

items.p: Substances with the same atoms joined in different patterns are called ____.
items.why: Isomers have the same number of each atom. They are different substances because their skeletons differ.

items.p: A cow gets energy from grass, but a person cannot. Both grass and rice are chains of glucose rings. Explain.
items.a: Rice is mostly starch, and human enzymes can cut starch into glucose. Grass is mostly cellulose, where every second ring is turned over. Human enzymes do not fit it. Microbes in a cow's stomach have enzymes that do.
items.why: A strong answer says the rings are the same but the join is different. It says an enzyme fits one kind of join.

items.p: Plan a test to find out whether a white powder from the kitchen holds carbon chains. Say what result you expect.
items.a: With a grown-up, heat a tiny pinch on a foil-covered tawa beside a pinch of salt and one of sugar. If it turns black like the sugar, it holds carbon chains. If it stays white like the salt, it probably does not.
items.why: A strong answer includes something to compare with, such as salt and sugar. It says what each result would mean.

items.p: Polythene is built like candle wax, but a candle is soft and a milk packet is tough. Explain the difference.
items.a: Both are chains of carbon and hydrogen. A wax chain has about 25 carbon atoms. A polythene chain has many thousands. Very long chains tangle and hold each other along their length, so the material is tough.
items.why: A strong answer says the atoms are alike and the length differs. It links length to how strongly chains hold each other.

items.p: Burning petrol and breathing both put carbon dioxide into the air. Why is the carbon from petrol a bigger problem?
items.a: The carbon you breathe out was taken from the air by a plant a short time ago. So it only goes round. The carbon in petrol was buried for millions of years. Burning it adds carbon to the air that was not there before.
items.why: A strong answer separates carbon that goes round quickly from carbon that was locked away for a very long time.

items.p: Could there be living things built on something other than carbon?

views.says: No. No other atom makes so many strong chains, branches and rings. Life needs that variety.
Perhaps. We know only one kind of life. On a very cold world with no water, other chemistry might work.
It depends on what we call living. If we look only for carbon life, we will find only carbon life.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about bonds. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer uses the facts about four bonds and strong chains. It may say that one example is too few to be sure.
items.why: Nobody knows the answer. A strong answer uses the chemistry of this lesson and admits what is not known.

items.p: Draw a ring of six carbon atoms. Add hydrogen atoms until every carbon atom has four bonds.
items.a: Six C atoms joined in a closed loop by six lines. Each carbon atom uses two bonds in the ring and holds 2 H atoms. That is 12 H atoms in all.
items.why: A strong drawing gives every carbon atom exactly four lines. A ring has no ends, so no atom holds 3 hydrogen atoms.
items.art: A blank box with the letters C and H shown in a small key at the side.

quiz.p: Why can carbon atoms build long chains?
quiz.why: A carbon atom holds two neighbours and still has two bonds free. The bonds between carbon atoms are strong, so the chain lasts.

quiz.p: What is the black solid left when sugar is heated strongly?
quiz.why: Heat drives the hydrogen and oxygen out of sugar. A black solid that is mostly carbon stays behind.

quiz.p: Which of these stays white on a hot tawa?
quiz.why: Salt holds no carbon. Sugar, atta and paper are built on carbon chains and rings, so they char.

quiz.p: Which list holds only forms of the element carbon?
quiz.why: Charcoal, graphite and diamond are carbon atoms joined in different ways. The other lists hold other elements or mixtures of atoms.

quiz.p: What do cooking gas, petrol and candle wax have in common?
opts: All are chains of carbon and hydrogen
All are made by plants today
quiz.why: All three are hydrocarbons. They differ in the length of the carbon chain.

quiz.p: Candle wax is a solid and cooking gas is a gas. What is the main reason?
quiz.why: A wax chain has about 25 carbon atoms and a cooking gas molecule has 1 to 4. Long chains hold each other strongly.

opts: A long chain of glucose rings
quiz.why: Plants join hundreds or thousands of glucose rings into one starch chain.

quiz.p: Cotton and cornflour are both built from glucose rings.
quiz.why: True. Cotton is cellulose and cornflour is starch. Both are chains of glucose rings, joined in different ways.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT built on carbon chains?
quiz.why: Glass is made from sand, which is silicon and oxygen. Wood, plastic and cotton are carbon chains.

quiz.p: How does a mango tree get carbon?
opts: Leaves take carbon dioxide from air
quiz.why: Leaves take in carbon dioxide and join the carbon into glucose, using light.

quiz.p: Substances found in living bodies can be made only by living bodies.
quiz.why: False. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from a mineral salt. Chemists now make sugars, vitamins and medicines.

quiz.p: Five carbon atoms can form three different liquids. How do the three differ?
opts: Their atoms are joined in different patterns
They have different numbers of atoms
quiz.why: All three have 5 carbon and 12 hydrogen atoms. One is a straight chain, one has a branch and one is a cross.

applications: Oil refineries separate petroleum by chain length. Short chains become cooking gas, middle chains become petrol and diesel, and the longest become wax and road tar.

Medicines are carbon molecules built to an exact shape. Asima Chatterjee, a chemist in Kolkata, studied carbon molecules from Indian plants. She developed medicines from them for epilepsy and malaria.
Charcoal is used in water filters. Its surface is full of tiny holes, and many unwanted molecules stick there.
Cooks use starch chains to thicken food. A spoon of cornflour or rice flour thickens a soup or a payasam when it is heated.
Carbon fibre is made of thin threads of carbon atoms joined in sheets. It is lighter than steel and very strong, so it is used in aircraft, racing cycles and rockets.
Scientists read the age of old wood, cloth and bone from one rare kind of carbon atom. It slowly disappears after a living being dies.

open_questions.q: How did carbon molecules first come together into something alive?
open_questions.why_open: Simple carbon molecules form easily, even in space. Nobody has yet shown every step from such molecules to a living cell.

open_questions.q: Must living things be built on carbon?
open_questions.why_open: Every living being found so far is carbon-based, but we have looked closely at only one planet.

open_questions.q: How many different carbon molecules are possible?
open_questions.why_open: The number is far greater than the number of stars we can see. Chemists have made only a tiny share, so most have never existed.

open_questions.q: Can microbes learn to eat all our plastics?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016 scientists in Japan found a bacterium who breaks down the plastic of water bottles. Most other plastics still have no known eater.

open_questions.q: Where can we safely put the carbon dioxide from burning fuels?
open_questions.why_open: Trees, soil, the sea and rock all take some up. Nobody yet knows how to store enough of it, cheaply and for long enough.

maths.problem: In One Bond or Four, a chain of 1 carbon atom held 4 hydrogen atoms. A chain of 2 held 6, and a chain of 3 held 8. How many hydrogen atoms will a chain of 4 hold? How many will a chain of 10 hold?
maths.answer: A chain of 4 holds 10 hydrogen atoms. A chain of 10 holds 22.
maths.explain: Each extra carbon atom adds 2 hydrogen atoms, so the numbers go 4, 6, 8, 10. So there are 2 hydrogen atoms for every carbon atom, plus 2 more for the two ends of the chain. For 10 carbon atoms, 10 times 2 is 20, and 20 plus 2 is 22.
maths.context: In One Bond or Four you drew chains of carbon atoms and filled every spare bond with a hydrogen atom.
maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you know a molecule you have not drawn. Chemists use this rule to write the formula of any chain.

maths.problem: In Five Carbons you found 3 skeletons for 5 carbon atoms. Chemists have counted the others: 4 atoms make 2 skeletons, 6 make 5 and 7 make 9. Do the numbers go up by the same amount each time? Will 8 atoms make more or fewer than 12?
maths.answer: No. The steps between the numbers are 1, 2 and 4, so they keep growing. 8 atoms will make more than 12. The real number is 18.
maths.explain: From 2 to 3 is a step of 1. From 3 to 5 is a step of 2. From 5 to 9 is a step of 4. The next step should be bigger than 4, so the answer is more than 13. It is 18.
maths.context: In Five Carbons you joined coins with matchsticks to find every different skeleton for five carbon atoms.
maths.why_maths: Looking at how fast a pattern grows shows why carbon makes millions of substances. Each extra atom adds more new skeletons than the one before.

maths.problem: In The Black Inside, 8 things were heated and 5 turned black. All 5 came from plants. The other 3 did not come from plants. Draw two circles: 'came from a plant' and 'turned black'. Where does each thing go? What do you notice?
maths.answer: Sugar, atta, cotton thread, paper and onion skin go in both circles. Salt, baking soda and the coin go in neither. No thing is in only one circle.
maths.explain: Every thing that came from a plant turned black, and every thing that turned black came from a plant. So the two circles hold exactly the same five things. That is strong evidence that the two facts are linked.
maths.context: In The Black Inside a grown-up heated eight kitchen things on a tawa, and you recorded which ones turned black.
maths.why_maths: Two circles show at a glance whether two facts go together. Here they show that charring and coming from a plant go together.

maths.problem: Here are four boiling points from the game Chain Line. Methane boils at 162 degrees below zero and butane at 1 degree below zero. Pentane boils at 36 degrees and octane at 126 degrees. Which are gases on a 30 degree day in Chennai? Which would still be a gas at 10 degrees below zero in Ladakh?
maths.answer: On a 30 degree day, methane and butane are gases. At 10 degrees below zero, only methane is still a gas.
maths.explain: A substance is a gas when the air is warmer than its boiling point. 30 is above 1 below zero and above 162 below zero, but below 36 and 126. 10 below zero is colder than 1 below zero, so butane turns liquid there.
maths.context: In the game Chain Line you put carbon chains in order of length. The back of each card gave facts such as the boiling point.
maths.why_maths: Comparing numbers above and below zero tells you whether a fuel will be a gas or a liquid. That is why LPG sold for cold places has more propane in it. Propane boils at a much lower temperature than butane, so it still works as a gas in the cold.

maths.problem: About 18 of every 100 kilograms of a human body is carbon. A child weighs 30 kilograms. How many kilograms of carbon does the child's body hold?
maths.answer: 5.4 kilograms, which is 5 kilograms and 400 grams.
maths.explain: For 100 kilograms the carbon is 18 kilograms, so for 10 kilograms it is 1.8 kilograms. 30 kilograms is 3 lots of 10, and 3 times 1.8 is 5.4.
maths.context: In The Black Inside, things made by plants left a black solid of carbon. A human body is built on carbon chains too.
maths.why_maths: A share out of 100 lets you work out the carbon in a body of any weight.

maths.problem: In Foil Packet Charcoal, wood became charcoal and smoke. A charcoal maker heats 100 kilograms of dry wood in a closed kiln and takes out 25 kilograms of charcoal. What fraction of the wood's weight left as smoke and gas?
maths.answer: Three quarters. 75 kilograms left as smoke and gas.
maths.explain: 100 take away 25 is 75. 75 out of 100 is the same as 3 out of 4. So three quarters of the weight left, and one quarter stayed as charcoal.
maths.context: In Foil Packet Charcoal, toothpicks heated in a tight foil packet came out as thinner black sticks. These are typical numbers for a charcoal kiln.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of the wood stays as charcoal. It explains why the sticks came out thinner and lighter.
