how_we_found_out.story: Two hundred years ago, chemists sorted substances into two kinds. Mineral substances, like salt, came from rocks. Organic substances, like sugar and urea, came from living bodies. Most chemists thought that only a living body could make an organic substance, with the help of a life force. In 1828 the German chemist Friedrich Wöhler heated a mineral salt called ammonium cyanate. White crystals formed. He tested them and found they were urea, the same substance as in urine. He wrote to his teacher that he had made urea without needing a kidney. One result did not change every mind, but more followed. In 1845 Hermann Kolbe made the acid of vinegar starting from carbon. Then chemists asked why carbon made so many substances. In 1858 the German chemist August Kekulé and Archibald Couper from Scotland each gave the same answer. A carbon atom makes four bonds, and carbon atoms bond to each other in chains. In 1865 Kekulé proposed that six carbon atoms could also close into a ring. In 1929 Kathleen Lonsdale used X-rays to show that this ring is real, flat and six-sided.
how_we_found_out.who: Friedrich Wöhler, Hermann Kolbe and August Kekulé from Germany, Archibald Couper from Scotland, and Kathleen Lonsdale in England
how_we_found_out.when: Wöhler made urea in 1828. Kolbe made the acid of vinegar in 1845. Kekulé and Couper published in 1858, and Kekulé proposed the ring in 1865. Lonsdale's X-ray work was published in 1929.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the substances of living things could be made only inside a living body, by a life force. Wöhler made urea from a mineral salt, and Kolbe made the acid of vinegar from carbon. So these substances follow the same chemistry as salt and rock.
how_we_found_out.art: A young chemist of the 1820s in a small laboratory, holding up a glass dish of white needle-shaped crystals to the light from a window.
how_we_found_out.context: Can the stuff of living things be made outside a living body? This card tells the true story of chemists who made it from plain minerals.

roots.context: In this lesson you found carbon inside sugar, cotton, paper, wood, fuel and plastic. Here we ask what it means that one kind of atom is the frame of so many things, including you.

deep_truth.truth: In The Black Inside, sugar, atta, cotton thread and paper each left a black solid when heated. That black solid is mostly carbon. Each carbon atom makes four bonds, so carbon atoms join into long chains and rings. That is why one element can be the frame of food, cloth, fuel and every living body.
deep_truth.habit: We treat food, cloth, fuel, plastic and living bodies as different kinds of matter. They share one frame, which is carbon atoms joined in chains and rings. What differs is the pattern of the joins.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Black Inside, five different things made by plants all left carbon, and salt left none. In Five Carbons, the same five atoms made three different skeletons. In One Ring, Three Materials, one ring made a sweet powder, a thickener and a fibre.

three.who_am_i: About 18 of every 100 kilograms of your body is carbon. Each of those atoms was in your food, before that in the air, and long before that inside a star.
three.what_is_life: Every living being we know builds their body on chains and rings of carbon. Plants take carbon from the air. Animals, including us, take it from plants and give it back with every breath.
three.what_is_this_world: The same carbon atom can be in the air, and then in a leaf. Later it can be in a child, and then in the air again. Sugar, wood, petrol and plastic are all built from carbon atoms joined in different patterns.

roots.thread: A grain of sugar, a cotton thread and a milk packet look like three unrelated things. Heat them and each leaves the same element behind. Their carbon atoms were made in stars, drifted through space and became part of the Earth. Plants take those atoms from the air and build them into chains. Every animal borrows the chains for a while. Many sages taught that the many things of the world are forms of one. The science here says something plain and close to that. A very large part of what you see is one kind of atom, joined in different patterns.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that by knowing one lump of clay, everything made of clay is known. The pot and the plate are names for shapes, and the clay is what is there.
teachings.link: One element, carbon, is shaped into sugar, wood and fuel. The text is speaking of one reality behind all things, and it is not speaking of an element. The likeness is in the way of looking: ask what a thing is made of, beneath its name.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding, the chapter 'Interbeing'
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you will see a cloud in it. Without the cloud there is no rain, without rain no tree, and without the tree no paper.
teachings.link: In The Black Inside, paper left carbon. That carbon was taken from the air by a tree, with water that fell as rain. The teaching and the chemistry trace the same path.

teachings.source: Primo Levi, The Periodic Table (1975), last chapter, 'Carbon'
teachings.teaching: Levi, a chemist, follows one carbon atom for hundreds of years. It leaves a rock and enters a leaf, a glass of wine and a man's body. It returns to the air many times.
teachings.link: This is the journey of the game Carbon Trail, told as a story. Levi says plainly that he made up the details. But every step he describes is one that carbon atoms really take.

science.text: Carbon atoms are made inside old stars and thrown into space when the stars die. The carbon in every living body on Earth came from such stars.
All life found so far is built on carbon chains, and all of it shares one family tree.
Whether life must be built on carbon, or could be built on something else, is not known.

other_view.view: Sharing an element says very little. A diamond, a plastic bag and a child all hold carbon, yet they have almost nothing else in common. What makes each thing what it is lies in the exact pattern of its atoms. On this view the differences are as real as the sameness, and matter more.

practice.title: One breath of carbon
practice.say: Sit still and hold one hand in front of your mouth. Breathe out slowly and feel the warm air. That breath carries carbon atoms that were part of your food. Now look at a plant, or at a tree outside the window. Their leaves are taking carbon from the air right now. Breathe out five more times, slowly. Each time, think of where one of those atoms might go next.
practice.kid: Hold a hand near your mouth. Breathe out slowly. That breath carries carbon from your food. Look at a plant. Breathe out five more times.

ask: In The Black Inside, white sugar left black carbon. Was the sugar hiding the carbon, or is 'black' only how carbon looks when it is alone?
A carbon atom was in the air, then in rice, then in you, and will be in the air again. At which moment was it yours?
A diamond and the black on a dosa are the same atoms in different patterns. Which matters more for what a thing is: its atoms or its pattern?

playtest: Every experiment, activity and game was reasoned through step by step, for a family in a city flat. None has been tried at home yet. The Black Inside (core) needs an old tawa, foil and eight tiny pinches from the kitchen. A grown-up heats them for 8 minutes with the exhaust fan on. Sugar, thread, paper and onion skin should turn black well within that time. Atta is slower and may stop at dark brown, so the steps say to record what really happens. Salt can crackle and jump. The steel coin may pick up a faint yellow or blue tint, which is not charring. One Ring, Three Materials (core) needs glucose powder or sugar, cornflour and cotton wool. With 2 level teaspoons in 100 millilitres, the cornflour thickens clearly just before boiling. If you use table sugar, tell your child that sugar is two rings joined, not one. One Bond or Four (core) needs only paper and a pencil. Chain Line (core) needs the 12 cards cut out. Foil Packet Charcoal and The Drawing Stick need a gas stove, tongs and a grown-up. They make smoke for a few minutes, so open a window. If the sticks are brown inside, they need more heating. Keep the packet closed for the full 10 minutes, or the charcoal may start to glow. These two cannot be done on an induction stove. There, The Black Inside needs a flat steel pan, lined with foil. Five Carbons, Paper Chain Starch, Carbon Trail and The Carbon Hunt need only things already at home. These are coins, matchsticks, paper and a die. No part needs a garden.
